screens.title: State Management and Navigation in React Native
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how React Native components keep track of changing data, how to run side effects such as fetching or logging, and how to move between app screens using a stack-based navigation model. We begin with the fundamental idea of component state: a local data value that drives what a component renders and updates the UI when changed. Then we introduce the useEffect hook, which runs code in response to renders and state changes, controlled by a dependency array. Finally, we show how to wire these concepts together with React Navigation: wrapping the app in a NavigationContainer, creating a Stack Navigator, and passing simple parameters between screens. As a concrete orientation, you'll build a small counter to observe state updates and a two-screen to-do flow to practice passing data and updating lists. Along the way we'll highlight common mistakes, like missing dependency arrays in effects or updating state without using a functional update when relying on previous values. By the end you should be able to manage local state safely, run controlled side effects, and navigate between screens while sending and receiving simple parameters. Consider this chapter the toolkit for making static screens interactive and connected.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › State & Navigation
State Management and Navigation in React Native
Build interactive screens using hooks, and move between them with React Navigation's stack pattern.

This module shows three practical skills: adding local state with useState, performing controlled side effects with useEffect, and wiring a simple stack navigator to move between screens while passing parameters. You'll see code examples, common pitfalls, and a short hands-on plan to build a to-do flow.

Coming up: a counter demo, effect patterns, and a two-screen to-do example that demonstrates navigation params and lifecycle behavior.

Explore Key Topics
useState
Component-local state for UI values like counters and form inputs.
useEffect
Run side effects and control when effects re-run with a dependency array.
Navigation
Stack-based screens, navigate with params, and access route data on the destination.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Live-coding style: code first, then run and reflect.
Visual Summary
State drives UI
Change state, re-render component.
Effects manage work
Run code after render and control when with dependencies.
Stack navigation
Push screens onto a stack and pass simple params between them.
Quick plan
Start with a counter to practice useState, add useEffect for logging, then scaffold a two-screen to-do flow to practice navigation and passing params. Watch for dependency array issues and prefer passing IDs over large objects when navigating.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have several practical skills. First, you will manage component-local state using the useState hook, initializing values and updating them safely even when updates depend on prior state. Second, you will use the useEffect hook to run side effects such as logging or data fetching, and you will control when effects run by using dependency arrays correctly. Third, you will set up a basic Stack Navigator using React Navigation, wrapping your app in a NavigationContainer and declaring screens with createStackNavigator. Finally, you will pass simple parameters between screens and read them on the destination using the route prop. Each objective pairs a capability with why it matters: keeping state correct prevents wrong UI, using effects properly avoids infinite loops or missed updates, navigation organizes user workflows, and passing only IDs or small params keeps navigation predictable. Together these skills let you build interactive, multi-screen apps that respond to user input and external data with predictable behavior.

screens.title: What is Component State?
screens.narratorSegment: Component state is mutable data local to a functional component that influences what the component renders. Unlike props, which come from a parent, state is owned and updated inside the component and triggers a re-render when changed. Think of state as the memory of a component: it holds values like a counter, the current text in an input, or a flag indicating loading. A concrete example is a counter initialized to zero. When the user taps an increment action, the state changes to one, and the displayed number updates. A common misconception is to treat state as synchronous or immediately available after calling the setter; in React Native the setter schedules an update and it may batch with other updates. Another misunderstanding is placing unrelated data in component state when it belongs in higher-level state or persistent storage. The practical significance is simple: keep UI-driven, ephemeral data in component state and update it through the provided setter. Key takeaway: state is local, reactive, and should be updated in patterns that avoid stale values. Ask yourself: does this value only affect this component's rendering, or does it belong higher in the app?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is Component State?
Definition and role

State is mutable data local to a functional component. When you update it with the setter returned by useState, React schedules a re-render so the UI reflects the new value.

Common misconception

Calling the state setter does not guarantee immediate synchronous access to the new value; updates may be batched.

Key Takeaway
Keep ephemeral UI data in component state and lift it only when multiple components must share it.
Concrete example: Counter
// App.js
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { Text, View } from 'react-native';

export default function CounterApp() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // component-local state
  // setCount(prev => prev + 1) when updating based on previous value
  return (
    <View>
      <Text>Count: {count}</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
This code shows initializing state and rendering it. Use the setter to schedule updates. For updates based on prior state, use the updater function to avoid stale reads.
Analogy
State is like a component's private notepad. Update it, and the component redraws itself with the new notes.
Pro tip
Group related values in objects only when updates are batched carefully; prefer separate state for unrelated values.
Check your understanding
If two sibling components need the same value, where should the state live? (Hint: lift it up.)

screens.title: useState Hook — Basics and Example
screens.narratorSegment: The useState hook lets a functional component hold local, reactive values. You call useState with an initial value and receive a pair: the current value and a setter function. In practice, you often use it for UI numbers, booleans, or strings. A clear example is the counter app: initialize count to zero, render it in a Text element, and provide handlers that call the setter. When the new value depends on the previous one, use the functional updater form, passing a function that receives the previous value and returns the new one. This prevents race conditions when multiple updates are scheduled close together. A common mistake is to write setCount(count + 1) in contexts where count may be stale; prefer setCount(prev => prev + 1) when relying on the old value. Practically, useState is lightweight and ideal for component-specific, ephemeral data. When many components must read or write the same piece of data, consider lifting state up or using higher-level state management. Try the counter: observe updates, then refactor the increment to the functional updater and compare behavior under rapid updates.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › useState Hook — Basics
Counter example
// App.js
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { View, Text } from 'react-native';

export default function CounterApp() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // initialize

  const increment = () => setCount(prev => prev + 1); // safe update
  const decrement = () => setCount(prev => prev - 1);

  return (
    <View>
      <Text>Count: {count}</Text>
      {/* UI controls would call increment/decrement */}
    </View>
  );
}
This code shows the pattern: useState returns [value, setter]. Use the updater function form when the new value is derived from the previous one.
Supporting points
  • State updates schedule re-renders; they are not always immediate.
  • Functional updates avoid stale reads in rapid updates or async contexts.
  • Keep state minimal—derived values can be computed from state when rendering.
Common mistake
Using setCount(count + 1) in a handler that may run multiple times quickly can lead to missed increments. Use the prev form instead.

screens.title: Functional Updates vs Direct Updates
screens.narratorSegment: Updating state can be done in two syntactic ways, but they behave differently in concurrent situations. The direct form calls the setter with a new value computed from the current variable, for example setCount(count + 1). The functional updater passes a function to the setter that receives the previous value and returns the new one: setCount(prev => prev + 1). The functional updater is robust when multiple updates queue before a render because it always uses the most recent previous state. In asynchronous handlers, timers, or batched event sequences, the direct form can read a stale count and overwrite other updates. A concrete exercise: trigger three rapid increments; compare results using direct updates and functional updates. You should observe missed increments with the direct form and correct increments with the functional form. A common misconception is to assume setters are synchronous; they are not. Key takeaway: prefer the functional updater whenever the new value depends on the old value to keep updates correct under concurrent scheduling. Functional Updates vs Direct Updates means when new state depends on previous values, pass an updater function to the setter to avoid stale reads and lost updates.. In practical terms, when to use updater functions to avoid race conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Functional Updates
Direct update
// direct update
setCount(count + 1);
This reads the current count variable. If multiple updates happen before a render, this value may be stale.
Functional updater
// functional updater
setCount(prev => prev + 1);
This always receives the latest previous state, ensuring increments are correct even when updates are batched.
Try this
Trigger three quick increments and compare which approach yields three increments consistently.
Pitfall
Using direct updates in async callbacks can quietly drop updates; tests may hide the issue outside rapid interactions.
Key Takeaway
When the new state depends on prior state, use the updater form to ensure correctness.

screens.title: useEffect — Performing Side Effects
screens.narratorSegment: useEffect is the hook you use to run code after a component renders. Effects are for side effects—work that interacts with the outside world or needs to run after a render, such as logging, fetching data, or subscribing to events. By default, an effect runs after every render, but you can control its timing through the dependency array. An empty array runs the effect only once after the component mounts, similar to componentDidMount. Including variables in the array runs the effect again whenever any of those variables change. Always consider cleanup: return a function from your effect to unsubscribe or cancel timers. A common mistake is omitting the dependency array, which may cause the effect to run on every render and produce infinite loops if the effect updates state. Another mistake is including objects or functions in the array that change on each render; prefer stable references or list the minimal dependencies. Practical example: log the count whenever it changes using useEffect with [count] as the dependency. This gives you controlled side effects without unnecessary re-runs. useEffect — Performing Side Effects means use useeffect for after-render work and dependency arrays to limit when effects run; include cleanup to avoid leaks.. In practical terms, control when effects run with dependency arrays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › useEffect — Side Effects
Logging when count changes
// Example: log count changes
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

function CounterApp() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    console.log('Count has changed to:', count);
    // cleanup not needed for simple logging
  }, [count]); // runs when 'count' changes

  return null; // UI omitted for brevity
}
The effect runs after each render in which count changed. Use the dependency array to precisely control effect triggers and avoid extra work.
Supporting notes
  • Empty dependency array: run once after mount.
  • No array: run after every render (dangerous for heavy work).
  • Return a cleanup function to unsubscribe or cancel timers.
Common mistake
Including non-stable values (like new inline functions or objects) causes effects to re-run each render. Memoize or list minimal dependencies.

screens.title: Dependency Arrays — Patterns and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency arrays are the control mechanism for effects. An empty array runs an effect once after the initial render — useful for one-time setup like fetching initial data. A specific array with listed variables runs the effect whenever any of those variables change, which is useful for reacting to user input or state changes. Omitting the array makes the effect run after every render, often leading to unnecessary work and sometimes infinite loops when the effect updates state that triggers another render. A typical pitfall is including values that are re-created every render, such as inline objects or functions, which forces the effect to run repeatedly. Another pitfall is forgetting to clear subscriptions or timers in the cleanup, leading to memory leaks or duplicate event handlers. Practically, list only the necessary dependencies and stabilize references when appropriate. If your effect needs to run once, use an empty array. If it must respond to changes, list those dependencies explicitly. Always test effects by changing inputs and verifying that the effect runs only when expected. Dependency Arrays — Patterns and Pitfalls means use the dependency array to control effect timing; avoid missing arrays or unstable dependencies that cause excessive re-runs.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Dependency Arrays
Empty array []
Runs once after initial render. Use for setup or one-time fetches.
Specific deps [a, b]
Runs when any listed variable changes. Use to react to particular state changes.
No array
Runs after every render. Often undesirable and may cause loops.
Example pitfall: listing an inline object or function as a dependency will usually trigger the effect every render because those references are new each time. Solutions include memoizing functions or moving stable values into state or refs.
Pro tip
When uncertain, list the minimal set of dependencies and test. Use ESLint rules for hooks to surface missing dependencies.
Warning
Effects that update state without careful dependency lists are a common source of infinite render loops.

screens.title: Intro to React Navigation and Stack Navigator
screens.narratorSegment: React Navigation provides an extensible approach to moving between screens in React Native. The fundamental steps are install the core packages, wrap your app in a NavigationContainer, create a Stack Navigator with createStackNavigator, and declare individual Stack. Screen entries. The NavigationContainer manages the navigation tree and state; Stack. Navigator defines the stack behavior where each pushed screen sits on top. HomeScreen receives a navigation prop with methods like navigate and goBack, while the destination screen receives both navigation and route props—route contains params passed during navigation. A typical setup includes the install commands and a simple App. js that returns NavigationContainer with Stack. Navigator and two screens. Common mistakes include forgetting to wrap the app in NavigationContainer, which prevents navigation from functioning, or mis-typing screen names when calling navigate. Practically, start with names that match your navigation calls and pass small params—prefer IDs and fetch larger data on the destination to keep navigation light. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › React Navigation Setup
Install and basic App.js
// App.js
import * as React from 'react';
import { NavigationContainer } from '@react-navigation/native';
import { createStackNavigator } from '@react-navigation/stack';

const Stack = createStackNavigator();

export default function App() {
  return (
    <NavigationContainer>
      <Stack.Navigator initialRouteName="Home">
        <Stack.Screen name="Home" component={HomeScreen} />
        <Stack.Screen name="Details" component={DetailsScreen} />
      </Stack.Navigator>
    </NavigationContainer>
  );
}
NavigationContainer

screens.title: navigation and route props — Methods and Params

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › To-Do App Walkthrough
TodoListScreen (state + effect)
// TodoListScreen.js (excerpt)
const [todos, setTodos] = useState([{id:'1', text:'Learn hooks'}]);

React.useEffect(() => {
  if (route.params?.newTask) {
    const { newTask } = route.params;
    setTodos(current => [...current, { id: String(current.length + 1), text: newTask }]);
    navigation.setParams({ newTask: undefined });
  }
}, [route.params?.newTask, navigation]);
This effect appends a new task when the param arrives and clears it to avoid duplicates on future focuses.
AddTaskScreen (send small param)
// AddTaskScreen.js (excerpt)
const [taskText, setTaskText] = useState('');

const handleSave = () => {
  if (taskText.trim()) {
    navigation.navigate('TodoList', { newTask: taskText });
  }
};
Pass the new task as a small param. The list screen integrates it into its state and becomes the single source of truth.
Key Takeaway
Keep authoritative data in one place and use navigation params for small, transient handoffs between screens.
Pro tip
Use navigation.addListener('focus') to refresh data when the screen becomes active, especially if data can change elsewhere.
Watch out
Do not pass large objects or entire arrays as params; prefer identifiers and fetch or reconstruct heavy data on the destination.

screens.title: Lifecycle of Functional Components
screens.narratorSegment: Functional components do not have lifecycle methods in the class-based sense, but lifecycle-like phases emerge from renders, state, props, and effects. A render occurs when props or state change. After a render, effects scheduled for that render run. If an effect updates state, another render is scheduled and the cycle continues. This means you should avoid effects that unintentionally cause state updates every time they run, because they can create render loops. For one-time initialization, useEffect with an empty array runs only once after mount. For responding to prop or state changes, include those values in the dependency array. Cleanup functions from effects run before the next effect and on unmount, which is useful for unsubscribing or clearing timers. A concrete example: subscribe to a device event in an effect and return an unsubscribe function in the cleanup. Misconception: assuming that setting state in an effect immediately changes the value synchronously in the same render; instead it schedules a new render. Key takeaway: reason about the render → effect → possible render loop cycle to keep behavior stable and predictable.

Lifecycle phases

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how React Native components keep track of changing data, how to run side effects such as fetching or logging, and how to move between app screens using a stack-based navigation model. We begin with the fundamental idea of component state: a local data value that drives what a component renders and updates the UI when changed. Then we introduce the useEffect hook, which runs code in response to renders and state changes, controlled by a dependency array. Finally, we show how to wire these concepts together with React Navigation: wrapping the app in a NavigationContainer, creating a Stack Navigator, and passing simple parameters between screens. As a concrete orientation, you'll build a small counter to observe state updates and a two-screen to-do flow to practice passing data and updating lists. Along the way we'll highlight common mistakes, like missing dependency arrays in effects or updating state without using a functional update when relying on previous values. By the end you should be able to manage local state safely, run controlled side effects, and navigate between screens while sending and receiving simple parameters. Consider this chapter the toolkit for making static screens interactive and connected.

By the end of this chapter you will have several practical skills. First, you will manage component-local state using the useState hook, initializing values and updating them safely even when updates depend on prior state. Second, you will use the useEffect hook to run side effects such as logging or data fetching, and you will control when effects run by using dependency arrays correctly. Third, you will set up a basic Stack Navigator using React Navigation, wrapping your app in a NavigationContainer and declaring screens with createStackNavigator. Finally, you will pass simple parameters between screens and read them on the destination using the route prop. Each objective pairs a capability with why it matters: keeping state correct prevents wrong UI, using effects properly avoids infinite loops or missed updates, navigation organizes user workflows, and passing only IDs or small params keeps navigation predictable. Together these skills let you build interactive, multi-screen apps that respond to user input and external data with predictable behavior.

This second objectives slide breaks the practical skills into narrower capabilities and common pitfalls to watch for. You will learn functional state updates—how to use the updater function form to avoid race conditions when new state depends on prior state. You will learn to control effect execution using dependency arrays, and to implement cleanup when subscribing to external events. You will see how the navigation prop methods like navigate and goBack work, and how the route prop exposes params. Finally, you'll practice integrating these pieces in a small to-do app that demonstrates returning results from one screen to another and updating a list on focus. Each objective explains why it matters: functional updates prevent stale values, dependency arrays avoid infinite loops, and passing IDs keeps navigation lightweight. This prepares you for real apps where state, side effects, and navigation interact.

Component state is mutable data local to a functional component that influences what the component renders. Unlike props, which come from a parent, state is owned and updated inside the component and triggers a re-render when changed. Think of state as the memory of a component: it holds values like a counter, the current text in an input, or a flag indicating loading. A concrete example is a counter initialized to zero. When the user taps an increment action, the state changes to one, and the displayed number updates. A common misconception is to treat state as synchronous or immediately available after calling the setter; in React Native the setter schedules an update and it may batch with other updates. Another misunderstanding is placing unrelated data in component state when it belongs in higher-level state or persistent storage. The practical significance is simple: keep UI-driven, ephemeral data in component state and update it through the provided setter. Key takeaway: state is local, reactive, and should be updated in patterns that avoid stale values. Ask yourself: does this value only affect this component's rendering, or does it belong higher in the app?

The useState hook lets a functional component hold local, reactive values. You call useState with an initial value and receive a pair: the current value and a setter function. In practice, you often use it for UI numbers, booleans, or strings. A clear example is the counter app: initialize count to zero, render it in a Text element, and provide handlers that call the setter. When the new value depends on the previous one, use the functional updater form, passing a function that receives the previous value and returns the new one. This prevents race conditions when multiple updates are scheduled close together. A common mistake is to write setCount(count + 1) in contexts where count may be stale; prefer setCount(prev => prev + 1) when relying on the old value. Practically, useState is lightweight and ideal for component-specific, ephemeral data. When many components must read or write the same piece of data, consider lifting state up or using higher-level state management. Try the counter: observe updates, then refactor the increment to the functional updater and compare behavior under rapid updates.

Updating state can be done in two syntactic ways, but they behave differently in concurrent situations. The direct form calls the setter with a new value computed from the current variable, for example setCount(count + 1). The functional updater passes a function to the setter that receives the previous value and returns the new one: setCount(prev => prev + 1). The functional updater is robust when multiple updates queue before a render because it always uses the most recent previous state. In asynchronous handlers, timers, or batched event sequences, the direct form can read a stale count and overwrite other updates. A concrete exercise: trigger three rapid increments; compare results using direct updates and functional updates. You should observe missed increments with the direct form and correct increments with the functional form. A common misconception is to assume setters are synchronous; they are not. Key takeaway: prefer the functional updater whenever the new value depends on the old value to keep updates correct under concurrent scheduling. Functional Updates vs Direct Updates means when new state depends on previous values, pass an updater function to the setter to avoid stale reads and lost updates.. In practical terms, when to use updater functions to avoid race conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

useEffect is the hook you use to run code after a component renders. Effects are for side effects—work that interacts with the outside world or needs to run after a render, such as logging, fetching data, or subscribing to events. By default, an effect runs after every render, but you can control its timing through the dependency array. An empty array runs the effect only once after the component mounts, similar to componentDidMount. Including variables in the array runs the effect again whenever any of those variables change. Dependency arrays are the control mechanism for effects. An empty array runs an effect once after the initial render — useful for one-time setup like fetching initial data.
